newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia's gold awaits investment, new rules.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia's gold awaits investment, new rules.

text.p: Gold is plentiful in the hills of the remote Magadan province in Russia's Far East, but local officials blame Moscow for making it unprofitable for many firms to mine the metal.

Last week, Moscow eased its rules to allow certain Russian banks to export bullion, ending a government monopoly on such sales. But officials in the Magadan region, which produces 20 to 25 percent of Russia's gold, said only full liberalisation of the market would help the local mining industry.

"It will be profitable for banks, but for gold producers it won't help," Deputy Governor Vecheslav Kobets told Reuters on Monday. "Under these new rules, local gold producers would have to sell gold at prices as much as 10 percent cheaper to banks."
That could still be more attractive than selling to the state, which in the past has paid late or not at all.
Moscow began mining gold in the Magadan region in the 1930s, using forced labour in an isolated region where temperatures fall to -60 Celsius in the winter.
But after the 1950s, many Soviet workers volunteered to work here, enticed by pay rises and other bonuses. Today gold mining accounts for 70 percent of the region's tax base.

Until recently, all mines had to sell their output to the government, which is a chronic late payer. As a result, many of the roughly 200 local mining firms pay workers three to six months late, officials say.

Such woes reduced output to about 20 tonnes of gold last year, down from an average of 40 tonnes a decade ago and 50-60 tonnes annually after 1945, Alexander Fesik, the governor's press secretary, said.
"Only the government has the right to buy gold, but they aren't paying for it -- it's a bandit's racket," he said.

Private business gets in on the act by buying gold on the side from miners and mining companies. Last year, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov described what he called the "total criminalisation of the gold-mining industry".
But Kobets said, "As long as the market is not open then everyone will hold some gold to the side." He added, "But this practice will be curtailed with the liberalisation of the market."

Compounding the region's problems is the realisation it has already mined much of its most accessible gold from rivers --so-called placer gold -- and needs large investment to mine gold deep in the ground.

"Historically, 95 percent of the 3,000 tonnes of gold accumulated from Magadan region since the 1930s has come from rivers," said Ilya Rozenblyum, chairman of the board of Omolon, a $228 million joint venture between U.S.-based Cyprus Amax Minerals and five Russian enterprises that this year started work at the country's largest gold mine.
"Now we must turn to more expensive mining...and we need to find investment," he said.

Yet since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, the trend has been toward smaller, less well-financed local gold companies forming out of old structures in the Magadan region, which has no rail lines and mostly dirt roads leading to mines.

"We need large corporate structures like a holding group that can invest in new and old enterprises," said Alexander Polyakov, director of Severovostokzoloto, which once organised the region's gold output and is now a contractor to newly independent mines. "Small enterprises cannot carry out the expansion of gold extraction."
Recent low gold prices and the Bre-X affair in Indonesia in which investors in the Canadian company lost millions of dollars has also hurt the market.
"We feel that some investors are feeling less interest from people raising capital because of the Indonesian Bre-X scandal," Kobets said. "This in turn affects companies' interest in us."

Across Russia, the world's fifth largest gold producer in 1995, when it produced 142 tonnes, other gold producing regions have suffered similiar woes. Various government and union officials see Russia's 1997 gold output in the range of 80-110 tonnes, down from the 122-124 tonnes reported in 1996.
